audience.programmeDescription: This English-taught degree studies living systems from molecules and cells to organisms and ecosystems.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The Groningen example follows Molecular Life Sciences. The UCR options emphasize molecular and biomedical biology, ecology and conservation, or brain and behavior.

cellNotes.text: Both introduce cell structure, inheritance and molecular mechanisms of life.
Both study how organ systems function and maintain physiological balance.
Both study the structure and function of biomolecules, including proteins, carbohydrates and lipids.
Groningen combines cell biology with microscopy. UCR covers cell structures, signaling and division in Molecular Cell Biology.
Both develop practical microbiology skills. UCR also uses protein and DNA techniques.
Both examine inheritance, gene regulation and genetic variation. UCR also studies how these mechanisms contribute to disease.
Groningen offers a dedicated cancer course. UCR covers neoplasia within a broader course on pathology and genetics.
Groningen integrates cell biology with immunology. UCR studies these subjects in separate courses.
Both study heredity, adaptation and evolutionary processes. Groningen also covers ecological foundations in this course.
Both examine how brain function relates to behavior. UCR includes comparative neuroanatomy.
Both develop academic skills such as working with sources and communicating evidence.
Both teach Python and computational problem-solving. Groningen uses biology applications.
Groningen analyzes biological sequence and related data. UCR introduces general data analysis and uses bioinformatics tools in the laboratory course.
Groningen models biological processes. UCR teaches numerical methods and machine learning with broader applications.
Both use statistical inference to analyze empirical research. UCR applies these methods to human behavior.
Groningen examines professional and ethical issues in biology. UCR studies ethical reasoning in a broader course.
Groningen offers a separate course in microbiology. UCR includes bacterial identification and culture in its Life Science Laboratory.
Groningen offers a separate course in metabolism. UCR studies energy pathways in Biochemistry.
Groningen develops laboratory research skills in a paired sequence with theoretical research.
Groningen develops theoretical research skills alongside the laboratory course.
Groningen studies the structure of biological molecules and its medical relevance.
Both study immune recognition and responses. UCR also examines how pathogens interact with host defenses.
Groningen offers a separate course in the organic chemistry of biological molecules.
Groningen combines specialist practicals before the major research project.
Groningen develops enzyme kinetics and thermodynamics. UCR introduces enzyme function and regulation in Biochemistry.
Groningen studies microbial communities and their interactions with hosts.
Choose an eligible 30 EC minor. Some life sciences minors include the Minor Congress within those credits.
Groningen offers an advanced course in techniques for studying molecules and large biological datasets.
Groningen studies epigenetic regulation and gene editing. UCR covers gene regulation and genetic technologies within broader courses.
Groningen requires a supervised project in the major. The UCR comparison shows optional independent research separately.

notes.text: Groningen develops a specialist sequence in molecular life sciences, including structural biology, microscopy and omics, followed by a required 15 EC project. The UCR options combine biology with data analysis, environmental science or psychology.

ACCPPDE101.name: Personal & Professional Development
ACCPPDE101.text: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.

DISDATA111.name: Introduction to Data Science
DISDATA111.text: Develops foundational skills in data visualization, cleaning and manipulation. Explores spatial and text data and includes hands‑on work with datasets from various disciplines.

DISDATA211.name: Machine Learning
DISDATA211.text: Machine Learning introduces methods for understanding data and making predictions, including linear regression, classification, resampling, shrinkage, tree-based methods, support vector machines and clustering. Real-world examples illustrate the methods, their strengths and limitations.

DISDATA212.name: Image Processing & Computer Vision
DISDATA212.text: Image Processing & Computer Vision studies how digital images are represented, processed and interpreted to recognise structures and objects. Topics include colour, image statistics, filtering, segmentation, feature detection, tracking and object classification. Practical work uses Python and OpenCV to develop and benchmark an image-recognition pipeline on previously unseen images.

DISDATA311.name: Neural Networks & Deep Learning
DISDATA311.text: Neural Networks & Deep Learning combines theory with practical Python, Keras and TensorFlow implementations. Students build and train networks, study backpropagation, regularisation and model evaluation, and apply deep learning to computer vision, time series and text, including transformers. Projects investigate prediction problems and report experimental results.

ENSDELT312.name: Governance of Sustainability
ENSDELT312.text: This course examines sustainability through the lens of governance: “a process of rule-making and collective decision-making that includes both governmental and non-governmental actors in shaping public policy” (Fenger & Bekkers, 2016). Taking this lens, we ask questions such as how are sustainability policies on the local, national, and international level made and enforced? Which actors represent which interests, and which are most influential? How is public opinion on sustainability shaped, and how does public opinion shape politics? What, at the end of the day, determines effective policy for sustainability? By the end of this course, you will have gained a deep appreciation of the complexity of the governance dimension of sustainability, and have developed the theoretical and practical understanding to critically assess mainstream policy decisions.

ENSECOL111.name: Introduction to Biodiversity
ENSECOL111.text: Introduces the diversity of living organisms, from bacteria and archaea to protists, plants, fungi and animals. Students examine evolutionary relationships, distinguishing characteristics and ecological roles. Practical work introduces microscopy, organism identification and biodiversity measurement, supported by a small project on a selected branch of the tree of life.

ENSECOL112.name: Conservation Biology
ENSECOL112.text: Examines human-driven biodiversity loss and approaches to conservation. Students study habitat destruction, overharvesting, invasive species, climate change and extinction, followed by conservation planning and species management. A local threatened-species project investigates conservation status and protection measures and develops a public-awareness flyer.

ENSECOL211.text: Examines evolution from genes to populations, including its history, mechanisms and theoretical and practical study. It develops evolutionary explanations of biological diversity and change.

ENSECOL212.text: Focuses on basic principles of ecology. Studies how environmental conditions affect organisms and examines ecological principles governing individuals, populations, communities and ecosystems, including ecological modelling and applied case studies.

ENSECOL311.name: Marine Biology
ENSECOL311.text: Studies ecological processes in marine environments such as estuaries, rocky shores and coral reefs. Examines human impacts and includes guest lectures, lab visits, excursions and field work, culminating in an essay.

ENSECOL312.name: Sustainable Farming & Innovation
ENSECOL312.text: Discusses environmental impacts of agriculture and explores sustainable agriculture approaches such as agroecology, organic farming, conservation agriculture, precision agriculture, sustainable livestock farming, agroforestry, permaculture, crop rotation, integrated pest management and sustainable supply chains.

ENSENVI111.text: Introduces Earth Science by focusing on interactions among the deep earth, lithosphere and hydrosphere. Highlights key cycles shaping Earth’s surface and includes indoor/outdoor labs and a multi‑day field excursion.
